extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemakers, counsel, policymakers, and researchers interested in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal analysis for agencies on how to process, evaluate, and respond to mass, duplicative, computer-generated, and malattributed public comments submitted under the Administrative Procedure Act and related statutes. Covers operational tools (de-duplication), legal risks (fraud, false statements, identity theft), and policy tradeoffs (substance vs. volume).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligation to respond to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency is not obliged to respond to every comment, only those that can be thought to challenge a fundamental premise. Agencies must 'respond in a reasoned manner to the comments received, to explain how the agency resolved any significant problems raised by the comments, and to show how that resolution led the agency to the ultimate rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no obligation to respond to comments per se; failure to respond is significant only insofar as it shows the agency’s decision was not 'based on a consideration of the relevant factors.' Agencies should focus responses on substantive issues and explain how significant concerns were resolved; courts will assess whether the agency considered relevant factors rather than whether every comment got an individual reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over volume (comments are not a vote)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public comment process is 'not a vote.' Agencies are under 'no obligation to take the approach advocated by the largest number of commenters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts have sometimes considered the number of comments in non-rulemaking contexts or particular inquiries (e.g., NEPA controversy), generally agencies should evaluate the substantive content of comments rather than tabulate pro/anti counts. Congress could provide guidance on when to treat volume or sentiment as relevant, but absent that, agencies should prioritize substantive evidence and analysis over sheer numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of relying on form comments
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general bar against agencies relying on information contained in form comments; courts have held 'there is no reason the Secretary was not entitled to rely on such letters in promulgating the regulations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on form letters is permissible; coordinated or pooled submissions 'sharing the same opinion' do not necessarily undermine their intended show of support. However, if an agency ignores categories of comments that offer differing views, that may be problematic. Agencies should consider substance and whether form comments add materially to the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and sophistication of comments as a determinant of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical literature finds influence depends on degree of sophistication in comments and the source of the comment; business/industry comments tend to be 'meticulously drafted, argued, and researched' whereas many citizen letters are short and lack technical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and researchers should weigh comments differently according to the evidence and data they provide. Hard data and substantive analysis are afforded greater weight; agencies may alter proposals based on well-supported submissions but are less likely to change course due to low-substance mass submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency approaches to opinions expressed in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewed agency officials report three approaches: (a) opinions are irrelevant—only factual content matters; (b) opinions are relevant to political perception and may affect agency actions or roll-out; (c) opinions are relevant insofar as they express popular sentiment and may inform leadership decisions, though not as the sole factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may reasonably adopt differing internal policies about the weight of expressed opinions, but should avoid making sentiment the sole basis for regulatory choices. Documenting how opinions were considered can help explain agency decisions in the preamble to a final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems raised by mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass campaigns often produce many duplicate or near-duplicate comments that impose real costs on agencies and add little substantive content; they can distort regulators’ perception of public opinion and lead to agency cynicism about the comment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should be aware that comment submitters are self-selected and not representative of the broader public. Consider the potential for manufactured salience and weigh mass campaign inputs accordingly; agencies may want policies to manage resource burdens and to preserve the integrity of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of de-duplication (de-duping) software
rubrics_metrics.description: De-duping software scans electronic comments, compares each to others, identifies degree of overlap, and groups comments that appear to derive from a common source (e.g., 90% identical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duping can massively decrease processing burdens by batching identical or nearly identical comments. It only analyzes words and order and may miss synonym-replaced text. Only electronic comments are directly processable; paper comments may be OCR'd first with variable integrity. Agencies choose thresholds (e.g., 90%, 50%) and must set policies about what overlap qualifies a comment as part of a mass campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting de-duping thresholds and implementation variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies set the overlap threshold (e.g., 90%) at which comments are flagged as likely part of a mass campaign; agencies vary in tools—some use FDMS-built tools, others agency-owned programs, contractors, or permit processors to use ad hoc tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No agency appears to require 100% overlap. Agencies must decide policy tradeoffs (false positives/negatives) when choosing thresholds and whether to adopt system-wide tools or decentralized practices. Documenting the chosen threshold and rationale can aid defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unique or partially unique additions in batched comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When participants add unique information (e.g., a sentence explaining personal impact) agencies generally review the unique information even if the identical content is batched and treated as a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duping reduces marginal processing time for identical iterations to near zero, but partially unique comments require more attention and may not be flagged depending on the overlap threshold. Agencies should inspect added language in near-identical submissions to determine whether it adds substantive, new information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting and public display practices for mass-submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies do not post all iterations of comments received on Regulations.gov if they qualify as part of a mass comments campaign; certain agencies post only a representative example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may choose to post representative examples to reduce redundancy on public portals, but should ensure that the public record preserves materially unique submissions and that posting practices are consistent with transparency obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malattributed comments: definition and distinct harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments involve a direct falsehood about identity and may harm not only the notice-and-comment process but also third parties whose names have been used; some characterize malattributed comments as a form of identity theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should treat malattribution as distinct from mere duplication: it raises legal and policy issues including possible criminality, the need for DOJ referrals, and potential harms to named individuals. Agencies should consider investigatory and remedial options, balancing practical enforcement likelihood and evidentiary hurdles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential criminal statutes applicable to malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible criminal prohibitions include fraud, making false statements, computer crime, identity theft, mail/wire fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, obstructing agency proceedings, and related statutes (e.g., 18 U.S.C. §§ 1001, 1028, 1030, 1341, 1343, 371).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of these statutes to malattributed comments is uncertain and legally complicated. Agencies should be skeptical about criminal prosecutability in many cases because elements like justifiable reliance, materiality, or an attempt to obtain money/property may be lacking. Agencies considering referrals should evaluate whether the statutory elements can be satisfied in a given instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud-elements analysis in the context of malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard definition of fraud has five elements: (1) a false statement of a material fact, (2) knowledge that the statement is untrue, (3) intent to deceive the alleged victim, (4) justifiable reliance by the alleged victim, and (5) injury to the alleged victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattributed comments may satisfy some elements (false statement), but courts may find difficulties proving agency reliance on the false identity, materiality of the misattributed identity, and tangible injury to the agency required for typical fraud charges. Agencies should assess these elements prior to concluding that criminal fraud applies.
